summary: Updates RFC 4733 with event codes for telephony signals used in channel-associated signalling when carried in the telephony event RTP payload. It replaces the assignments from RFC 2833 section 3.14, some of which were deprecated, and widens coverage of signalling systems. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This adds new codes for the beeps and signals of old phone lines so they can be sent in internet calls without confusion.

subtitle: Event codes that let old-style phone trunk signalling ride inside RTP between gateways.

tldr.problem: When a telephone trunk is replaced by an RTP stream, audio encoding destroys robbed-bit signalling and can disturb in-band multi-frequency tones, so the signalling that sets up calls gets lost.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5244 assigns telephone-event codes to the signals of Signalling System No. 5, R1, R2, ABCD bit states, continuity tones, trunk unavailability and metering pulses, so gateways can send them as events instead of as audio.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 4733 and supersedes the signalling events of RFC 2833 section 3.14, but is fully backward compatible with RFC 2833 only for full ABCD-bit signalling.

today: RFC 5244 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4733, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It supersedes the channel-associated signalling events of RFC 2833 section 3.14.

sections.title: The RTP Trunk Problem
sections.content:
Trunks are the media paths between telephone switches. Over the years, several protocols were built that use tones and electrical conditions on each individual trunk to set up calls. RFC 5244 extends the telephony events of RFC 4733 to cover the signals of these channel-associated signalling systems that are still in use in the telephone network.

The target is the RTP trunk application: RTP replaces a normal circuit-switched trunk, and the PSTN signalling is carried between two gateways without being signalled in the IP network. Each gateway encodes the audio with a codec such as G.723.1 or G.729. That encoding destroys in-band signalling carried in the least-significant bit (robbed-bit signalling) and may interfere with multi-frequency (MF) digit tones.

Gateways may swap roles from one call to the next, so each must be able to both send and receive every signal it implements. The RFC also warns that its descriptions of the signalling systems are incomplete and give only context for the event definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: If you squash a message into a smaller shape, little details can get squashed away. The phone company's secret beeps get squashed when voice is compressed, so this sends them as labelled notes instead.

sections.title: The Event Codes at a Glance
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC lists every event it defines. Tone events carry a frequency and a volume; state events (ABCD) and the metering and trunk events carry no volume. The codes fall into blocks: MF digits and KP/ST signals in 123 to 128 and 129 to 137, ABCD states in 144 to 159, A-bit and AB-bit states in 206 to 211, R2 forward signals in 176 to 190 and R2 backward signals in 191 to 205.

The RFC replaces the assignments of RFC 2833 section 3.14. Some of those were deprecated in Appendix A of RFC 4733 because they were ambiguous, erroneous or redundant. Because the IANA registry for telephony event codes was set up by RFC 4733 and not by RFC 2833, older assignments appear there only if they were reaffirmed in RFC 4733 or in an update such as this one.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a big phone book where every beep and every flag gets its own number, so everyone looks it up the same way.

sections.title: Signalling System No. 5 and R1
sections.content:
Both systems have line signals, which acquire and release the trunk, and register signals, which pass digits forward. No events are defined for No. 5 line signalling itself. Implementations MAY use the AB-bit events to carry it, and if they do they MUST map both 2400 Hz and 2600 Hz present to code 208, 2400 Hz only to 210, 2600 Hz only to 209, and neither to 211. For R1 line signals, implementations MAY use the A-bit events: 2600 Hz present is code 206 and no signal is code 207.

Register signals are pairs of tones. Implementations carrying them in the telephone-events payload MUST use code 128 for digit 0 and codes 129 to 137 for digits 1 to 9. For SS No. 5, code 123 is Code 11, 124 is KP1, 125 is KP2, 126 is ST and 127 is Code 12. For North American R1, code 123 is KP3P or ST3P, 124 is KP, 125 is KP2P or ST2P, 126 is ST and 127 is KP' or STP. The receiver decides whether 123, 125 or 127 means a KPx or an STx signal from its position in the sequence.

In No. 5 register signalling all signals except KP1 and KP2 last 55 ms, KP1 and KP2 last 100 ms, and pauses between signals are always 55 ms. R1 allows a large tolerance for when register signalling starts after the start-dialling line signal, so a sender MAY wait to report a KP until it has completed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each button on an old phone made a pair of beeps. Here every pair of beeps gets a number, and the other side plays the right pair when it sees the number.

sections.title: Signalling System R2
sections.content:
R2 is described in ITU-T Recommendations Q.400 to Q.490, with many national variants. Its line signals are continuous, out-of-band, link by link and channel associated. Its register signals are multi-frequency, compelled, in-band and end-to-end. Implementations MAY use the A-bit or AB-bit events for R2 line signals. For analog lines, code 206 means tone-on and code 207 means tone-off. Digital R2 line signals use the same A and B mapping in both directions.

R2 register signalling is compelled: a tone plays until an acknowledgment for the next tone arrives. A forward signal is acknowledged by a backward signal, and a backward signal is acknowledged by the end of the forward signal. The same tone can mean different things depending on where it occurs in the sequence and on the country. To avoid an unmanageable number of events, the RFC only provides codes for the 15 forward tones (176 to 190) and 15 backward tones (191 to 205), and leaves the meaning to the signalling system.

A naive relay of R2 register signals across several exchanges and a gateway can cause unacceptably long call setup times and timeouts. In the worst case the relay point has to act as an exchange, ending the signalling on one side and reoriginating the call on the other.
sections.plainLanguage: R2 is a polite conversation: one side beeps until the other beeps back. The numbers just say which beep it was; the meaning depends on the conversation.

sections.title: ABCD Bits as Event Codes
sections.content:
ABCD signalling is a 4-bit system for digital trunks. It can be 16-state (all four bits), 4-state (A and B only) or 2-state (A only). The events are mutually exclusive states, and the most recent transition determines the current state. In ESF T1 framing the bits are robbed from frames 6, 12, 18 and 24; a D4 superframe carries only 4-state signalling; on an E1 frame signalling is in timeslot 16.

The state number is the used ABCD bits read as a binary number with A as the high-order bit, and state 0 maps to event code 144 up to state 15 at code 159. With only A and B, the codes are 208 for 00, 209 for 01, 210 for 10 and 211 for 11. With only A, code 206 is A=0 and code 207 is A=1. Separate codes exist because the default values of unused bits differ between transmission systems, so the receiving gateway fills them in from local configuration.

Because ABCD is a state rather than a changing signal, implementations SHOULD use triple redundancy: at a transition the same information is sent 3 times at an interval of 5 ms, repeating if another transition occurs, and after a period of no change it is sent every 5 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of four light switches that can each be up or down. Each combination of switches gets a number, and the sender repeats the number a few times so it is not missed.

sections.title: Continuity, Trunk Unavailable and Metering
sections.content:
Continuity tones test a circuit during call setup. For four-wire trunks a single 2000 Hz check-tone goes out and the remote switch loops it back; this MUST be event code 121. For two-wire trunks a 2000 Hz tone goes forward (code 121) and a 1780 Hz verify-tone comes back (code 122). The RFC notes that implementations often send a slightly different check-tone, for example 2010 Hz, because of aliasing problems with 2000 Hz.

The trunk unavailable event (code 175) says a trunk is out of service for the time in the duration field; a value of 1 second is RECOMMENDED. When the trunk becomes unavailable the event is sent three times with the same timestamp at an interval of 20 ms, and is retransmitted if the trunk is still unavailable when the duration ends. It avoids sending a continuous RTP stream for the whole downtime.

The metering pulse event (code 174) carries billing pulses. Each report MUST have both the M and E bits set, and senders must be ready to send the telephone-event and audio payload types at the same time. The retransmission interval is RECOMMENDED to be the lesser of 50 ms and the pulsing rate, but no less than the audio packetization rate.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the phone line's checkups: a test beep to see the wire works, a sign saying 'closed for repairs', and a click that counts how much the call costs.

sections.title: Congestion Considerations
sections.content:
Most of these signals tolerate longer durations, so under congestion a sender can lengthen the reporting interval. If a receiver is playing a tone and packets are late or lost, it is best to keep playing the tone until the next packet arrives, because stopping early can make the call setup fail while extended playout only adds delay.

Register signalling for SS No. 5 and R1/MF is the exception. Tones and silent gaps have specified durations with tolerances of the order of 5 to 10 ms, and tones last two to three packetization intervals (55/68 ms, with the initial KP at 100 ms). The receiver mainly needs to know which signal to play, and should play the specified durations rather than the reported ones. The sender should report a register signal as soon as it is identified, then update within 5 ms for reliability and send nothing more until the end of the tone. A larger receiver playout buffer improves reliability but lengthens call setup.
sections.plainLanguage: If the internet is busy, it is better to keep a beep going a bit too long than to cut it short, because a cut-off beep can make the call fail.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These events relate directly to setting up, billing and taking down telephone calls, so they face threats to both communications and system security. The attacks of concern are listed as confidentiality violations (monitoring of calling and called numbers), unauthorized connections through message insertion, hijacking of connections through insertion or man-in-the-middle modification, and denial of service to individual calls through insertion, modification, deletion or delay.

If confidentiality, authentication or integrity protection is needed, SRTP SHOULD be used with automated key management. Further considerations are in RFC 4733.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could listen in on who is calling whom, or send fake signals to make free calls. Locking the messages with SRTP stops that.
